7. Series

Watch infinite series converge or diverge through their partial sums, and master the convergence tests.

  • The Harmonic Series Diverges — The partial sums SnS_nSn​ follow ln⁡n+γ\ln n + \gammalnn+γ upward — very slowly, but without end.
  • The Euler–Mascheroni Constant — The harmonic numbers HnH_nHn​ diverge like ln⁡n\ln nlnn, but their gap γn=Hn−ln⁡n\gamma_n = H_n - \ln nγn​=Hn​−lnn settles at γ≈0.5772\gamma \approx 0.5772γ≈0.5772 — the secret is the convergent series ∑(1n−ln⁡(1+1n))\sum (\frac1n - \ln(1+\frac1n))∑(n1​−ln(1+n1​)).
  • The Basel Problem — Stack the terms 1n2\frac{1}{n^2}n21​ as 3D bars and watch the staircase of partial sums approach the plane at π26\frac{\pi^2}{6}6π2​ without ever touching it. Why π\piπ appears at all is only sketched at the idea level.
  • The Euler Product — Multiplying ζ(s)=∑n≥1n−s\zeta(s) = \sum_{n\ge 1} n^{-s}ζ(s)=∑n≥1​n−s by (1−2−s)(1-2^{-s})(1−2−s) sieves out the even terms, then (1−3−s)(1-3^{-s})(1−3−s) removes multiples of 3 — sieving leaves only the product over primes ∏p(1−p−s)−1\prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}∏p​(1−p−s)−1. Watch the partial product over the first kkk primes approach ζ(2)=π2/6\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6ζ(2)=π2/6.
  • Leibniz Series — The partial sums overshoot and undershoot π4\frac{\pi}{4}4π​ in turn, closing in from both sides. The gap between two neighboring partial sums is exactly the error bound.
  • Convergence Tests Toolbox — When the ratio rk=ak+1/akr_k = a_{k+1}/a_krk​=ak+1​/ak​ settles to a limit L<1L < 1L<1, the series converges — watch the ratios dive to 000 and 12\frac{1}{2}21​ in two series, and 1k2+1\frac{1}{k^2+1}k2+11​ tuck itself under 1k2\frac{1}{k^2}k21​ for the comparison test.
  • The Integral Test — For a decreasing positive function the rectangles lock above and below the curve: ∫1N+1f≤∑1Nf(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1f\int_1^{N+1} f \le \sum_1^N f(n) \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} f∫1N+1​f≤∑1N​f(n)≤f(1)+∫1N+1​f — series and improper integral share one fate. Move ppp to see the p-series fork.
  • Raabe's Test — When the ratio drifts to 1 and the ratio test surrenders, the finer quantity Rn=n(an/an+1−1)R_n = n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1)Rn​=n(an​/an+1​−1) settles above or below 1 and decides convergence.
  • Kummer's Test — Weighting the ratio by a positive auxiliary sequence (pn)(p_n)(pn​), the sign of Kn=pnanan+1−pn+1K_n = p_n\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - p_{n+1}Kn​=pn​an+1​an​​−pn+1​ decides convergence. pn=1p_n = 1pn​=1 recovers the ratio test, pn=np_n = npn​=n recovers Raabe's test.
  • Cauchy Condensation Test — Group the terms ana_nan​ into blocks [2n,2n+1)[2^n, 2^{n+1})[2n,2n+1): each block sum is sandwiched between condensed terms 2na2n2^n a_{2^n}2na2n​, so the original and condensed series share their fate.
  • Telescoping Series — Split each term into 1n−1n+1\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1}n1​−n+11​ and the neighbors cancel each other, leaving only the very first 1 and a vanishing tail.
  • Geometric Series: Filling the Square — Fill a unit square by always taking half of what remains: the gap halves at every step and the total becomes 1.
  • Wallis Product — Multiply the rational factors in one at a time and watch the running product swing above and below π2\frac{\pi}{2}2π​, closing in as the swings shrink.
  • Stirling's Approximation — On a log scale, n!n!n! and the Stirling approximation nearly coincide, and the relative error shrinks like 112n\frac{1}{12n}12n1​. Where π\piπ enters is only sketched at the idea level.
  • Grandi Series — The partial sums bounce between 1 and 0 forever, so this series has no sum. 12\frac{1}{2}21​ is only the average of the partial sums (the Cesàro mean), not a sum of the series.
  • Dirichlet's Test — The partial sums of sin⁡(kx)\sin(kx)sin(kx) wobble, trapped inside 1/∣sin⁡(x/2)∣1/|\sin(x/2)|1/∣sin(x/2)∣, and the 1/n1/n1/n weight sinking to 000 tames them into the convergent series ∑n=1∞sin⁡(nx)n\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin(nx)}{n}∑n=1∞​nsin(nx)​ — Dirichlet's test.
  • Abel's Test — If \\\sum a_n\ converges and \(b_n)\ is monotone and bounded, then \\\sum a_n b_n\ converges — the companion to Dirichlet's test. The difference: \(b_n)\ need not tend to 0.
  • Double Series and Fubini — Sum the grid by rows first or by columns first — with absolute convergence the answer is the same. ∑m,n1m2n2=(π26)2=π436\sum_{m,n} \frac{1}{m^2n^2} = \left(\frac{\pi^2}{6}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi^4}{36}∑m,n​m2n21​=(6π2​)2=36π4​. Conditional convergence lets the order change the answer.
